analysis.one_liner: Bans stock trading by federal officials, curbs the lobbying revolving door, and creates an independent ethics-enforcement agency.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, two weeks after its introduction with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar members of Congress, cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and other senior officials from owning or trading individual stocks and from serving on corporate boards. It would impose long bans on former officials becoming lobbyists, create an independent Office of Public Integrity to enforce federal ethics laws, and require officials and candidates to disclose their tax returns. It would also ban corporate PACs, ban forced arbitration, offer public financing for congressional and presidential campaigns, and tax lobbying spending. [S2, S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want a government that does not trade on its own decisions. The bill's stock-trading ban, tax-return disclosure, and revolving-door bans target the ways officeholders and their future employers can profit from public service. Its forced-arbitration repeal would let workers and consumers take companies to court, its public-financing provisions would let candidates run on small donations, and its donor-disclosure rules would expose the money behind lobbying and campaign spending. [S2, S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens, workers, and small-dollar donors

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress, cabinet secretaries, federal judges, and other senior officials from owning or trading individual stocks or serving on corporate boards, while allowing widely held index funds and a new Federal Employee Investment Account as replacements.

Institutes a lifetime lobbying ban for former members of Congress, Presidents, and agency heads, a 6-year ban for former corporate lobbyists entering government, and a 4-year hiring ban on giant banks and companies employing former senior officials, with penalties for companies that violate it starting at 1 percent of their net profit.
Requires the Supreme Court to follow the same ethics rules as other federal judges, tightens judicial gift rules, and creates procedures for handling misconduct complaints against judges.
Creates an independent Office of Public Integrity to enforce federal ethics laws across the executive and legislative branches, with public, searchable records of every waiver it grants.

Requires Presidents, Vice Presidents, members of Congress, and candidates to disclose tax returns and more financial information, and exposes more of the corporate money behind lobbying and elections.
Includes a 'Forced Arbitration Injustice Repeal' provision that would let workers and consumers sue companies in court instead of being forced into private arbitration.

Bans corporate PAC contributions, bans corporations from fundraising for candidates, bars big-donor ambassador appointments, and creates public financing for Senate and presidential campaigns built on small-dollar matching funds.
Imposes a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, bans contingent-fee lobbying, and requires disclosure of 'political intelligence' activity aimed at informing investors rather than the public.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations, lobbying firms, giant banks, and federal contractors would bear new taxes, disclosure requirements, hiring bans, and penalties measured against their profits. Incumbent officeholders would have to divest individual stocks, publish their tax returns, and face independent ethics enforcement. Taxpayers would fund the new enforcement agency and the public campaign-financing system. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate interests, lobbying firms, and officeholders

drawbacks.text: The divestment and revolving-door rules are broad: they bar senior officials from owning any individual security or closely held business and from private-sector work tied to their old agencies for years, which could deter experienced people from serving; the bill tries to soften this with a Treasury-run Federal Employee Investment Account for officials to park their investments in.

The bill concentrates major discretionary power in a new, unelected Director of the Office of Public Integrity, who would control registration, enforcement, and case-by-case waivers of several of the bans it creates.

The progressive tax on lobbying expenditures and the lifetime lobbying ban would face immediate constitutional challenge on First Amendment grounds, since courts treat petitioning government and political speech as protected activity.
Public campaign financing, the new enforcement agency, and the expanded investment accounts all require new federal spending, with appropriations authorization left to later Congresses.

At several hundred sections spanning lobbying, rulemaking, courts, campaign finance, and records law, the bill bundled far more than any single Congress could enact, and much of it reaches into areas with competing good-faith views on design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-integrity measures answer a real problem: officials trading stocks in industries they regulate and moving to lobbying firms afterward. The tradeoffs are real too — some provisions are very broad, the enforcement design hands large power to one appointed director, and parts would likely be litigated for years. The core stock-trading ban and revolving-door restrictions are achievable policies with clearer benefit-to-cost ratios than the bill's full scope.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced the bill on December 19, 2020, two weeks before that Congress expired; the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Elizabeth Warren introduced the Anti-Corruption and Public Integrity Act in the Senate on December 19, 2020.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The referral went to Finance because the bill includes a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, which gives the tax-writing committee jurisdiction over the bill.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lobbying industry, giant banks, federal contractors, and incumbent officeholders kept the existing rules in place, since none of the bill's restrictions took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbyists, large corporations, and incumbent officeholders

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2020, in the final days of the 116th Congress.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, took no action on the bill; the action history shows nothing after the December 19, 2020 referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: United States Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator other than the sponsor cosponsored the bill, and the Senate took no further action on it before the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party and was never debated or voted on, so the record shows no partisan split on it; it is a solo Democratic-sponsored measure that died in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and the political influence industry
industries.note: The bill imposes 6-year to lifetime revolving-door bans on former officials, bans contingent-fee lobbying, requires disclosure of political-intelligence work, and taxes lobbying expenditures progressively. Its death left the existing, lighter disclosure regime unchanged. [S3]

industries.industry: Giant banks and large financial firms
industries.note: The bill bars them from hiring former senior officials for 4 years with penalties starting at 1 percent of net profit, and bans their executives from serving on government boards after the fact. None of this took effect. [S3]
The bill would extend FOIA to them, require disclosure of their political spending, and ban hiring officials who oversaw their contracts for 4 years. None of this took effect. [S3]

industries.industry: Corporate campaign spenders and corporate PACs
industries.note: The bill bans corporate PAC contributions, bans corporations from fundraising for candidates, and requires disclosure of campaign-related disbursements and dark-money nonprofit donors. Its death left current campaign finance rules in place. [S3]
The forced-arbitration repeal would have ended the practice of requiring workers and customers to give up their day in court. The repeal never became law. [S3]
The bill would impose political-ad disclaimer and recordkeeping duties on platforms carrying election advertising, a compliance cost but not an existential one; nothing took effect. [S3]

industries.industry: Think tanks and tax-exempt 'dark money' nonprofits
industries.note: The bill requires donor disclosure and repeals IRS procedures that let certain nonprofits keep contributors confidential. It never advanced. [S3]

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior federal officials
industries.note: The bill bans their individual stock ownership and trading, requires their tax returns, and subjects them to an independent ethics enforcer with criminal anti-corruption provisions. Every one of these officials kept the existing, weaker rules because the bill died. [S2, S3]
